transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-08-10 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~55 mins | Attendees: Maya, Noah, Priya (Redwood); Amira, Jorge, Lena, Tom (OliveGrove)

Summary (auto): Discussed private onramp options, network topology, region restrictions, security controls and next steps.

00:00:03 Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we'll give a quick intro from our side — i'm maya, ae here at redwood inference, and with me is noah and priya from our engineering team. you guys good to go?
00:00:16 Amira Singh: yeah hi thanks, i'm amira, head of ml infra at olivegrove. we've been evaluating hosted vs private and we're leaning private because of data residency and audit controls.
00:00:28 Jorge Castillo: and i'm jorge, cloud architect — we'll be owning the peering and network design. we've got some constraints around regions and egress.
00:00:37 Noah Alvarez: great — quick agenda, we'll cover topology options (vpc peering vs transit gateway), private endpoint patterns, egress + allowlist, and then security / compliance notes, and close with next steps. sound ok?
00:00:48 Tom Beckett: yep, also interested in how rollback and failover would work for canary deploys when region is gated.
00:00:55 Maya Chen: good call, we'll touch on that.

00:02:05 Noah Alvarez: so high level, redwood private runs a control plane we can hand off, and a data plane that either sits in your vpc (private deployment) or in a peered vpc managed by redwood. there are two common patterns: full vpc peering or use of transit gateway for multi-account setups, and a private endpoints (privatelink) approach for minimal routing changes.
00:02:30 Jorge Castillo: quick question — for the transit gateway path, do you terminate in our account or your managed account? and how much route churn are we looking at when we add more zones or regions?
00:02:43 Priya Rao: typically we can deploy the inference nodes in a dedicated account and peer via TGW with route table propagation. the route churn is bounded — you add a route for the prefix and propagate, we can script the onboarding so it's not manual. but there is a stretch there: if you want full control we can co-locate agents in your VPC.
00:03:03 Lena Park: ok, and from a security pov we need that the data plane never traverses public internet and keys are customer-managed (kms). can you confirm kms integration and audit log availability?
00:03:15 Maya Chen: yes we support customer-managed KMS for model payload encryption at rest and in transit TLS. audit logs — we can forward request logs to your splunk/s3 depending on retention needs. there is an option for HSM integrations for FIPS workloads but that's part of private enterprise package.

00:04:40 Amira Singh: on regions — we have EU residency requirements. primary production must live in eu-west-1, and backups in eu-central-1. can we pin nodes to region and ensure no cross-border egress?
00:04:55 Noah Alvarez: absolutely we can pin model serving to specific regions. for failover we support regional DR but you can opt out of cross-region replication. the important bit is the traffic path: if you're using TGW peering in the same AWS org then it's within the cloud backbone; if you use a managed redwood account in another org we can do private link to avoid transiting public endpoints.
00:05:20 Jorge Castillo: how do private endpoints work operationally? do we create interface endpoints and you call back into them?
00:05:28 Priya Rao: yes, with privatelink we ask you to create interface endpoints for the services we expose. that keeps the traffic entirely in the AWS private network and avoids route table changes. downside: scaling many endpoints across many AZs can mean more endpoint ENIs to manage and limits you have to watch.
00:05:45 Tom Beckett: what's the egress IP situation? we need a fixed set of IPs to allow through our firewall to third-party data services.
00:05:53 Maya Chen: for private we can provide egress NATs or fixed egress IP ranges if we host the nodes in your VPC. if nodes are in our managed account, we can advertise a small pool of egress IPs and use NAT gateways — we'll need to exchange those IPs and update your fw rules.
00:06:12 Lena Park: and how about TLS and mTLS? we require client certs inside the vpc for service-to-service.
00:06:20 Noah Alvarez: we can support mTLS between your clients and our data plane; typical setup is mutual TLS for control-plane API calls. some customers front with an internal ALB/NLB and mTLS is terminated at their side, with internal trust established.

00:07:40 Jorge Castillo: latency numbers — if we pin to eu-west-1, what's typical 95th percentile for generation workloads? we have sub-200ms targets for short prompts.
00:07:51 Priya Rao: depends on model and batch sizing. for small 2-4 token completions on quantized 7b models we often see 50-120ms p95 on modern gpus in-region. if you choose dedicated pools we can further optimize latency and lower jitter.
00:08:10 Amira Singh: cost tradeoffs — dedicated vs hosted vs private in our VPC? we want predictability.
00:08:18 Maya Chen: Dedicated gives predictable throughput with reserved capacity (monthly commit). Private in your VPC is similar economically but you take more operational overhead (NAT/IP, KMS). Hosted is easiest but less control over residency. We'll send a cost comparison sheet.

00:09:45 Tom Beckett: regarding failover — if eu-west-1 goes down, can we fail to eu-central-1 but only after manual approval? we can't have automatic cross-border failover without legal ok.
00:09:57 Noah Alvarez: yes we support manual failover policies. Rollouts can be configured so canary in primary region only, and if you want we can configure hold gates so a human approves any cross-region shift.

00:11:20 Jorge Castillo: network addressing — we plan to use 10.12.0.0/16 for ml-prod VPCs. will that conflict with your managed ranges?
00:11:27 Maya Chen: we'll share our recommended non-overlapping ranges. if there's overlap we can use NAT-based proxies or we can deploy in your VPC to avoid that.

00:12:35 Lena Park: auditability: can we get token-level traces, request ids, and per-request latency logs shipped to our logging? retention needs to be 1 year for audit.
00:12:48 Priya Rao: yes token-level billing breaks down and we can emit tracing hooks; for retention of that size we typically ask customers to archive to their S3. note: redwood stores short-term traces for SLOs but long-term retention is offloaded.

00:13:55 Amira Singh: we may need to run a bench with our sample prompts and data residency constraints — how does that look operationally?
00:14:03 Noah Alvarez: generally we spin up a pilot cluster in your target region with the model of choice, load it with your prompts, and run a mixed workload sim. we'll need whitelisted IPs, VPC IDs, and a pilot user with credentials. benchmark usually takes 1-2 days to get representative numbers.
00:14:20 Jorge Castillo: do you have a sandbox automation script we can run for VPC onboarding?
00:14:26 Maya Chen: yes, we'll send a terraform module and a checklist for TGW/privatelink.

00:15:55 Tom Beckett: about network egress cost — if you host in our VPC, we avoid cross-account data transfer but still pay for NAT GW traffic — are there recommendations?
00:16:05 Noah Alvarez: we recommend using centralized NATs in a shared services VPC to reduce per-AZ NAT costs. if traffic is mostly internal to aws region, costs are lower. We can also use private link to minimize NAT egress.

00:17:30 Amira Singh: compliance questions: SOC2, iso27001, pen tests? we require vendor attestation and a copy of the latest SOC2 report before procurement sign-off.
00:17:41 Maya Chen: understood — we'll share our SOC2 report and pen test summaries; for private deployments we offer an expanded compliance pack and support for security questionnaires.

00:19:00 Jorge Castillo: one more on IP management — we prefer IP whitelisting with CIDR notation. will you provide a stable set of CIDRs for your egress?
00:19:10 Priya Rao: if we host in your vpc, you control the egress IPs. if we host in our managed account, we'll provide a small CIDR allocation used by our NATs and documented. note: sometimes cloud providers reassign public IPs; for strict policies we recommend privatelink + interface endpoints so no public egress is required.

00:21:30 Tom Beckett: about route propagation, we want to minimize route table entries. is the privatelink approach lightest?
00:21:38 Noah Alvarez: yes privatelink avoids adding many static routes; peering/TGW will add routes per prefix. So if you want minimal route changes and strict control, privatelink + interface endpoints is the preferred.

00:23:12 Amira Singh: how does logging for requests look with privatelink? will we still be able to see per-request metadata?
00:23:20 Priya Rao: yes, the traffic stays private but request telemetry can be pushed to your logging endpoint — we instrument the service to include request ids and metadata.

00:24:45 Jorge Castillo: are there hard limits on interface endpoint count per region? we run into soft limits often.
00:24:53 Maya Chen: aws has limits on endpoints per account/region — we'll share recommended quotas and help open service limits if needed.

00:26:00 Noah Alvarez: ops question — what's your desired SLA? is 99.9 enough or do you need 99.95/99.99 for certain workloads?
00:26:09 Amira Singh: for production LLM features we aim for 99.95. for internal tooling less. but SLA is less important than predictable latency.

00:27:35 Tom Beckett: regarding service mesh — some of our infra uses istio sidecars, does redwood integrate nicely with mesh traffic?
00:27:44 Priya Rao: yes we can integrate; many teams terminate at NLB and then talk to sidecars. there are a few patterns, and we can provide a sample config.

00:29:10 Jorge Castillo: question on identity — SSO/SAML for console access and fine-grained RBAC? we need auditable admin actions.
00:29:19 Maya Chen: we support SAML/SSO and org-level RBAC. for private deployments the console can be federated into your identity provider and admin events get logged.

00:30:40 Amira Singh: ok practically what's the onboarding timeline to pilot? we want to start pilot in 2 weeks.
00:30:48 Noah Alvarez: suppose we get CIDRs and whitelisted IPs in 3 days, we can spin a pilot in the eu-west-1 region within 7-10 days. total pilot time including benching is roughly 2 weeks.

00:32:05 Jorge Castillo: are there any gotchas with cross-account TGW attachment when accounts are in different orgs? we've seen permission headaches.
00:32:16 Priya Rao: yes cross-org TGW attachments require shared resource policies and sometimes manual acceptance by the TGW owner. for simplicity, privatelink is lower friction cross-org.

00:33:40 Tom Beckett: what about model weights and caching? we can't have weights leaving our VPC.
00:33:48 Noah Alvarez: we can host the model weights inside your VPC entirely, or use a read-only S3 in your account that our nodes mount via endpoint. KV cache sits in RAM on the inference nodes; if you need persistence we can use your redis or memcached inside your VPC.

00:35:12 Lena Park: on encryption in transit, do you support TLS1.3 and ability to rotate certs?
00:35:21 Maya Chen: yes TLS1.2/1.3 supported, cert rotation is available and we can integrate with your cert manager.

00:36:40 Amira Singh: procurement: pricing model for private deployment — is it usage plus infra or flat?
00:36:49 Maya Chen: typical is a mix: infra + mgmt fee for private, or reserved capacity for dedicated. we'll send a detailed quote after we scope the pilot size and throughput.

00:38:02 Jorge Castillo: any differences in debugging when using privatelink vs peering?
00:38:09 Priya Rao: with privatelink, flows are interface endpoint -> NLB -> service, so packet captures are on the endpoint ENIs. With peering/TGW, you can trace at route table level. Both debuggable but tools differ.

00:39:30 Noah Alvarez: ok, quick recap of recommended path given your constraints: since you require strict EU residency, prefer privatelink interface endpoints in eu-west-1 with nodes pinned to that region; avoid cross-region automatic failover, configure manual DR to eu-central-1. use customer-managed KMS, forward audit logs to your s3, and we'll provide a terraform onboarding module.
00:39:58 Amira Singh: that sounds good. can you also provide a minimal egress CIDR list we can pre-authorize?
00:40:06 Maya Chen: yes we'll provide a set of stable egress CIDRs and if needed recommend privatelink-only to avoid public egress entirely.

00:41:20 Tom Beckett: next steps?
00:41:25 Maya Chen: we'll do action items: we'll share the VPC onboarding repo (terraform), our SOC2 + security pack, and a proposed date for the benchmarking deep dive (we suggested 8/17). Jorge/Amira to share CIDRs, firewall rules, and pilot user creds.
00:41:45 Jorge Castillo: we'll get CIDRs and firewall rules by friday.
00:41:50 Amira Singh: i'll review the SOC2 docs and share procurement constraints.
00:42:10 Maya Chen: great. any outstanding risks or blockers?
00:42:20 Lena Park: only the procurement timing — procurement may delay until SOC2 is verified.
00:42:28 Maya Chen: understood. we'll prioritize the security pack to speed that up.

00:43:55 Noah Alvarez: one last technical note — if you need ultra-low-latency with pre-warmed KV caches, we can provision dedicated pinned nodes and warm caches with your prompt sets ahead of time. that's part of the optimize toolkit.
00:44:10 Amira Singh: that's interesting — we'll consider as part of the pilot.

00:45:00 Maya Chen: ok wrapping up, thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the artifacts in the next 24–48 hours.
00:45:08 Jorge Castillo: thanks all, bye.
00:45:12 Tom Beckett: bye.

(Transcript ends — auto summary and action item extraction appended.)
